Triggers.value: Specific body parts associated with the event
Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to sleep or lying in the dark

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: 'Always plan an escape route before entering a place' implies a persistent current external-danger / entrapment threat style that is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on intrusive sensory memory linked to the child's illness (body parts, darkness, songs; reliving, fragments, present-tense memory). For trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, this strategy is clinically much less coherent than avoidance/sleep delay, and it is not supported by any Threat or Appraisal items. Given the formulation, Triggers and Memory are strongly linked, but this item reflects a different syndrome focus (situational escape/safety behavior) not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes.

vignette: Kiet was forty when the night his son turned blue finally anchored itself in his chest. It began with a sudden fever at their Central Valley home, but by the time the paramedics arrived, his boy’s ribs were pressing sharply upward against a thin cotton shirt, the collarbones lifting with every labored breath. Kiet watched the color drain from his son’s face in the back of the ambulance, his own hand gripping the steering wheel until his knuckles whitened. He remembered the exact shape of his son’s throat, the quick flutter of a pulse there, and the sudden cry that had cut off into silence. When the boy was stabilized, Kiet sat beside the narrow bed for three days, certain that any shift in the monitors would mean the same suffocating panic returning. In the months that followed, the memory of those hospital nights did not settle quietly in the past. Sometimes, Kiet would be mending a fence line, and a fragment of his son’s breathing would surface without warning, vivid and immediate, before fading as quickly as it had come. Other times, the whole scene would return so completely that he was no longer standing in the sunlit field but leaning over a hospital mattress, his own breath syncing with the monitor’s steady beep. What frightened him most was the certainty that the threat was still there, waiting just beneath the surface. He had come to believe that his own body held the same vulnerability his son had possessed during that crisis, and he began watching his chest and throat as closely as he had watched his boy’s. The triggers of that ordeal followed him into his work and his home. When the morning radio played certain songs from the local Vietnamese station, the familiar melodies would catch in his throat, transporting him back to the quiet hum of the ward. He found himself standing in the feed room, the radio crackling, his fingers tracing the hollow of his collarbone until the song passed. Nighttime held its own particular weight. Waking in the dark had become a trial; the silence of the bedroom felt thick, and he would lie rigid, listening to the creak of the farmhouse settling, convinced that any sudden shadow in the corner was a sign of trouble. He avoided sleep when he could, not because he was tired, but because closing his eyes felt like stepping into the same uncertainty that had once paralyzed him. When he did lie down, he kept the hallway light on, watching the ceiling until his exhaustion finally pulled him under. Over time, these habits shaped his days. He delayed going to sleep until the house was completely still, sometimes sitting on the porch long past midnight, the cool California air doing little to quiet his mind. He began avoiding people more than he would have liked. Visits from neighbors or his wife’s friends felt like intrusions into a space that needed to remain predictable. He would answer questions with short nods, his eyes scanning the room as if checking for something unseen. He skipped the town market where children ran between the stalls, the sight of their quick, deep breaths making his chest tighten. At the farm, he worked through the quiet hours, mending irrigation lines and checking the crops before the heat rose, finding solace in the repetitive motion and the open sky. Now, at forty-two, Kiet’s wife has noticed how he moves through the house as though bracing for a storm that never quite breaks. The PCL-5 score of 76 from his recent screening reflects what he has lived: a mind that watches for danger, a body that holds onto past threats as if they are happening now. He is finally seeking help because the delayed sleep and the sudden fragments of memory have begun to blur the line between farm and hospital, leaving him exhausted and uncertain. What he hopes for is not the elimination of his vigilance, but the ability to let his son’s breathing return to its ordinary rhythm, to lie in the dark without counting the seconds, and to trust that the body, whether his or his son’s, can simply rest.
